title: AI agents describe and tag data-catalog columns, with stewards approving each
problem: Data lakes gain tables faster than stewards can document or classify them, so columns lack descriptions and sensitivity labels.
approach: Glyph, a production system of cooperating AI agents, writes column descriptions and assigns labels from a governed 275-label list, never reading values.
A data steward accepts or rejects every suggested column-tag pair; decisions feed weekly retraining.
Steward acceptance rose from 63.3% to 99.8% over six weeks (self-reported); the authors call this an association, not a cause.

title: Rules-first data classification with AI fallback that distils stable findings into rules
problem: Privacy controls need a reliable view of what each data asset is, and manual review cannot keep pace with AI-native products.
approach: Meta describes a hybrid classifier: versioned rules answer first, and an AI model handles only novel or ambiguous assets.
About 85% are answered by rules in milliseconds; about 15% go to the AI fallback at roughly 400 times the cost (self-reported).
People adjudicate reference labels and approve rule promotions; low confidence, judge disagreement or rare sensitive classes escalate to human review.

title: Instruction-driven Gemini labelling of Google Drive files, replacing admin-trained models
problem: Label-based data loss and retention policies only work on correctly labelled files, and labelling put a considerable manual burden on admins.
approach: Google announced an open beta in which Gemini applies classification labels to Drive files from administrator-written instructions, with no model training.
File owners and editors with label permission can accept or modify each Gemini-applied label; audit logs record decisions.
Google states it helps admins reach higher accuracy at scale; no figures published (vendor-published).

title: Plain-language sensitive-data search and credential scanning with an AI agent (preview)
problem: Searching for relevant data and finding out how it is protected is, in Microsoft's words, time-consuming, tedious and highly manual.
approach: Microsoft Purview's Data Security Posture Agent interprets plain-language requests, searches Microsoft 365 content and returns results with an AI-written risk analysis.
A second preview agent scans Microsoft 365 for exposed credentials and tracks remediation tasks on a board.
The requester reads the results and decides what to act on; Microsoft claims quick results, no figures (vendor-published).

title: AI-native platforms that find, classify and fix sensitive data across cloud
problem: Organizations do not know what sensitive data they hold or where; Varonis telemetry across 1,000 environments found only about one in ten companies had labelled files.
approach: Cyera customer stories describe agentless scanning to classify sensitive records, then clean-up; the pages say little about how AI contributes.
ChenMed resolved more than 32,000 data security issues across 30 policies; Paramount scanned trillions of records, billions sensitive (vendor-published).
Security and data owners decide which findings to remediate; Vetcor says tabletop exercises validated what data an attack would expose.

title: AI agent sorts data-loss alerts into urgency queues with written rationale
problem: Triaging and prioritising data loss prevention alerts is complex and time-consuming, and false positives and alert fatigue strain analysts.
approach: Microsoft Purview's Triage Agent reads alerts across Exchange, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and endpoints, analyses the files and sorts them, with an explanation.
Admins can add plain-language custom instructions (preview); Microsoft says prioritisation reduces triage time, no figures (vendor-published).
Analysts review each categorised alert and rationale and can overrule it through feedback.

title: Context-aware AI data-loss classification replacing pattern-matching to cut false alerts
problem: Legacy data loss prevention tools struggled with nuanced unstructured files and produced so many false positives that OpenWeb's team could not trust the alerts.
approach: OpenWeb replaced its tools with MIND, which the vendor says uses a proprietary AI engine to classify unstructured data with context.
OpenWeb's CISO: DLP effort 'probably a fifth' of before; a US financial institution's 16,000 false positives fell to 'just a handful' (vendor-published).
Human review is not described in detail; the bank's security, privacy and governance teams share a risk-driven programme.
who: OpenWeb, MIND, Cyera, unnamed US bank

title: Inline data-loss controls on prompts, pastes and uploads to generative AI tools
problem: Staff paste source code, regulated data and credentials into generative AI tools; only 29% of surveyed firms can routinely report what was sent.
approach: Microsoft Purview endpoint policies can warn or block users pasting sensitive information into third-party AI sites, and inspect prompts in supported apps.
A Hacker News commenter describes a proxy that tokenises personal data and blocks secrets.
Policy owners decide warn versus block; users may be shown a warning they can override. Baselines come from vendors and a survey.

title: Discover shadow AI use; block or steer unsanctioned AI apps and accounts
problem: Employees adopt AI tools outside security and procurement review, and AI features appear inside existing apps without governance being told.
approach: Netskope reports 90% of organizations block at least one generative AI app, and personal-account use fell from 78% to 47% (vendor-published).
OWASP recommends an allowed-tool policy, a central AI service catalogue with security and privacy review, and data loss controls.
Security and procurement owners approve the allowed-tool list and review new AI services. Akamai announced and then completed its LayerX acquisition.

title: Assess and reduce oversharing before and during rollout of AI assistants
problem: AI assistants surface content quickly, amplifying existing oversharing; Varonis reports 99% of 1,000 environments hold sensitive data AI can easily surface.
approach: Microsoft Purview's posture tool tracks AI activity such as oversharing and unusual access, and offers data risk assessments.
SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery removes chosen sites from organization-wide search and Copilot as a temporary control while permissions are fixed.
Admins choose which sites to restrict and decide on permission clean-up. The 99% figure is a baseline (vendor-published).

title: Agents propose and, with approval, fix exposed data such as public links
problem: Access and sharing problems are found in dashboards but fixed by hand, one object at a time.
approach: Microsoft says Purview's posture tool uses Security Copilot and AI agents to analyse access and sharing, prioritise risks and act on them.
Actions include removing public sharing links, applying data loss policies or revoking permissions.
Administrators review, approve or customise automated actions, which are always audited. No outcome figures published (vendor-published).

title: Enforce labels and user access when AI assistants retrieve content, including indexes
problem: In an AI system, retrieved passages, prompts and tool output sit in one flat space with no internal access control, and classification rules rarely reach embeddings or backups.
approach: Microsoft says supported AI apps withhold content from users lacking access; encrypted labels need view and extract rights.
OWASP recommends labels follow every derivative, retrieval enforce per-document access control, and erasure cover derived copies.
A research prototype, ARBITER, filters retrieval queries by role at 85% accuracy (independent); OWASP recommends human review of high-impact corpora.

title: AI-guided workflow turning privacy requirements into enforceable data controls using data lineage
problem: Turning written privacy requirements, especially purpose limitation, into controls across large data systems is slow, error-prone and hard to validate.
approach: Meta engineers described an AI-guided workflow that breaks requirement text into implementable tasks and walks data lineage to find affected datasets.
It suggests enforcement and monitoring points and tracks each requirement through to verification.
The session reports where automation helped and where human judgment stayed essential, including misinterpretations and lineage gaps (self-reported); no figures.

title: AI detection of privacy-relevant code patterns in pull requests, using retrieved examples
problem: Many privacy failures come from ordinary coding choices; Default Grant Access, where access is allowed unless blocked, is hard for static analysis to catch.
approach: Microsoft reported deploying AI detection of Default Grant Access in pull requests at scale, then adding retrieved examples from known incidents.
The retrieval version found more than twice as many confirmed issues; false positives did not significantly improve (self-reported).
Code reviewers see detections inside the pull request review and confirm issues.

title: AI first drafts of privacy impact assessments, reassessments and evidence reviews
problem: Product teams often lack privacy expertise, and privacy teams manage manual assessments with 'assessment fatigue' and constrained budgets.
approach: OneTrust's Winter '26 release drafts reassessment answers from earlier evaluations and reviews evidence files, giving a summary, justification score and gaps.
Academic work tests the idea: Privy gives non-experts a first draft of risks, which 13 privacy experts rated high quality (self-reported).
Privacy staff validate AI-completed fields and review scores; experts still make high-impact decisions.

title: Idea: AI detection of personal data to redact prompts, logs and text
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: AI providers mask personal data in conversations, yet most detectors and benchmarks target self-contained records, not multi-turn dialogue.
approach: Researchers compare rule-based, encoder and AI detectors on benchmarks; a rule-based detector recalled only 0.07 on high-sensitivity categories (independent).
No detector reaches full coverage without substantial false positives, and all degrade under shifted inputs.
Human checkpoints are not specified in the research; reviewers would set thresholds and spot-check misses.

title: Idea: middleware trimming AI-agent tool calls to the minimum personal data needed
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: AI agents routinely put sensitive data into tool-call arguments beyond what the tool needs, sending it to third parties.
approach: ToolMinimize, a research prototype, intercepts tool calls and removes, generalises, substitutes or truncates argument values.
In tests, 81-88% of tool calls held unnecessary sensitive data by default; the middleware cut privacy cost 81.2-92.0% (independent).
Human checkpoints are not specified in the paper.

title: Idea: plain-text policy files let an AI model block risky coding-agent prompts
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: coding agents accept free-form prompts that may hold credentials or proprietary data, and existing controls are rigid.
approach: PolicyGuard, a research prototype, intercepts prompts and classifies them with an AI model guided by a plain-text policy file non-engineers can edit.
It reached a 96.5% block rate with 3.0% false positives on the authors' test set (independent).
Policy owners edit the policy file; blocking decisions are automated.

title: Giving AI agents governed access to certificate and cryptographic inventory
problem: Certificate lifespans are stepping down toward 47 days by 2029, so manual certificate management does not scale.
approach: AppViewX announced a Summer 2026 release with a Model Context Protocol server giving AI agents governed access to certificate inventory and metadata.
The company calls this a foundation for later AI-driven certificate lifecycle operations; no figures published (vendor-published).
Human checkpoints are not specified; the release exposes read access only.

title: Testing AI-generated private synthetic financial data against direct synthesis
problem: Privacy-protected synthetic data is hard to build for high-dimensional tables, so teams ask whether AI simulators could help.
approach: Capital One researchers condensed customer attributes into private profiles under differential privacy and seeded an AI generator to produce transactions.
Direct synthesis significantly outperformed the AI approach on fraud-detection utility and fidelity; no figures given (self-reported).
Privacy engineers evaluate fidelity and utility before use.

title: Private analytics on AI chatbot use: enclave-based AI releasing only noisy totals
problem: Understanding real-world generative AI use is needed to improve products, but conventional analytics risks exposing sensitive user input.
approach: Google's Provably Private Insights combines secure enclaves, AI models that interpret unstructured data inside them, and differential privacy for aggregation.
Used in the Pixel Recorder app to classify transcripts; production runs a Gemma 3 4B model on CPUs inside secure enclaves.
No outcome figures published (self-reported); human checkpoints are not specified in the abstract.
